summary: Initial cost/economics discovery. Customer runs a suite of LLM features (summary, generation, reranking) at Summit Ridge Capital and is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private. Key priorities: keep average unit cost under budget, preserve p95 latency SLA for queries, and ensure data residency/KMS for sensitive models. Discussed batching, prefix/KV caching, quantization, and committed reserved capacity tradeoffs. Agreed next steps: Redwood to send cost model and run a Dedicated sizing follow-up.
topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 14:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Laura Bennett (VP Eng, Summit Ridge), Tom Alvarez (Head of MLOps), Priya Shah (CTO)
---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, Uh Ethan is with me on the SE side. Quick intros?
[00:18] Laura Bennett: Hi yeah Laura here, VP Eng at Summit Ridge. We're mainly owning the production ML infra and the LLM features.
[00:24] Tom Alvarez: Tom, Head of MLOps, I look after infra, costs, compliance.
[00:28] Priya Shah: Priya here, CTO, interested in overall costs and security posture.
[00:33] Ethan Park: Great. The goal for today's call is cost econ, so per-token pricing, batching/caching levers and whether Hosted, Dedicated or Private makes sense given your volumes.
[00:45] Maya Chen: Quick agenda: we want to understand your query mix, target latency/SLA, budget per token, and then run through how caching/batching and Reserved Dedicated pricing affect effective unit cost.
[01:05] Laura Bennett: Perfect. High level - we run three main LLM features: user-facing generation (conversational summaries), backend batch rerank for candidate scoring, and an embedding pipeline for search. Roughly 70% of tokens are generation, 20% batch rerank, 10% embeddings.
[01:27] Tom Alvarez: Volume is around 20M tokens/day currently, peaks up to 35M on heavy days; average request length ~120 tokens. Our target p95 latency for user-facing is 350ms, but we'd accept up to 600ms for some internal flows. Budget-wise we want to keep blended cost below ~$0.0008 per token on average, or about $800 per million tokens - that is the internal target.
[02:00] Ethan Park: Okay that's great context. Just to set expectations: hosted open-model pricing we typically present as a baseline; Dedicated (reserved) gives you predictable throughput and lower unit cost under commit. Private (VPC/on-prem) is higher ops but gives full control and best isolation.
[02:23] Laura Bennett: Can you walk through an example of how batching and KV/prefix caching change the effective per-token price?
[02:31] Ethan Park: Sure. Crudely, if you can use prefix caching - for example repeated system prompts or shared prefixes - you can avoid re-computing attention for the prefix and only pay for new tokens. On our runtime that's a big delta for chat-heavy workloads. With batching, the GPU amortizes kernel startup costs so per-token GPU compute and memory bandwidth cost falls.
[02:57] Maya Chen: I'll throw some numbers - these are illustrative: a hosted baseline for an open LLM might be around $0.75 to $1.50 per million tokens depending on model/latency. With batching + prefix/KV caching you can effectively reduce that by 20-50% depending on hit rates. Dedicated reserved capacity with commits and quantized models can get you further savings - sometimes 2-3x cheaper than baseline if your utilization is high.
[03:30] Tom Alvarez: (mutter) those ranges help, yeah. How confident are you in the 2-3x number? If our traffic is bursty and not perfectly steady, utilization drops.
[03:40] Ethan Park: Totally. That's the key tradeoff. For Dedicated we model utilization with autoscaling and burst pools. You can set a committed baseline that covers steady state and allow burst to host or burst to cloud - so effective cost depends on percent of tokens served from committed GPUs vs burst. We usually run a break-even analysis: given your steady tokens/day and p95 needs, at what commit level does Dedicated become cheaper than Hosted.
[04:06] Priya Shah: What about quantization or model variants? We have some internal tests on 7B vs 13B models. Does Redwood support INT8 or other quantized paths in Dedicated?
[04:18] Ethan Park: Yes, our runtime supports mixed precision and int8/4 quantization profiles. There's a small accuracy tradeoff sometimes, but for many prompt families it's negligible. Quantization reduces memory and enables higher batch sizes, which pushes down cost per token. We'll show quantization effect on the cost model spreadsheet.
[04:41] Laura Bennett: On privacy - KMS, SOC 2, audit logs - we need to know what is achievable on Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. We have regulatory constraints on some data fields.
[04:52] Maya Chen: Hosted supports encryption-at-rest and transit, SOC 2 controls, and we have customer-managed keys on higher tiers. Dedicated and Private give you more control: VPC peering, BYOK with HSM/KMS integrations, and optionally an on-prem package for air-gapped setups. We'll attach security whitepapers.
[05:12] Tom Alvarez: Excellent. Back to cost: for our 20M tokens/day avg, if we wanted to target $0.0008/token, what levers should we prioritize?
[05:22] Ethan Park: Priorities: 1) maximize cache hit rate for generation prefixes, 2) increase batching for backend reranks (these are good for batching), 3) use quantized model variants for lower-criticality flows, 4) consider Dedicated commit sized to cover ~60-80% of steady-state if your traffic is stable. Also consider model selection: smaller models for fallback or non-critical flows.
[05:49] Laura Bennett: Can you show a short sample calc on the call?
[05:52] Maya Chen: Sure - rough calc: assume hosted baseline $1.00 per million. With caching (40% effective token saving) and batching (20% saving) that compounds to roughly 1 - (0.6 * 0.8) = 52% of baseline, so effective $0.52 per million. Dedicated with commit and quantization might then bring it to ~ $0.20-$0.30 per million at high utilization. Again these are ranges and depend on actual workloads.
[06:24] Tom Alvarez: Understood. The math makes sense. That would meet our $0.0008/token target (which is $0.8 per million) if Hosted w/ caching already at $0.52 per million, actually above - hmm, wait, our target was $0.0008 token = $0.8 per thousand? (brief confusion)
[06:40] Priya Shah: Sorry real quick - to clarify units, our target is $0.0008 per token equals $0.8 per thousand tokens? I think we meant $0.8 per million tokens.
[06:51] Laura Bennett: Right, we mean $0.8 per million. So if numbers are $0.52 per million, that's below our target.
[06:58] Ethan Park: Great, good catch - unit mismatch happens a lot. We'll put clean numbers in the spreadsheet so there's no ambiguity.
[07:06] Maya Chen: A few clarifying Qs: how bursty is your traffic by hour, do you have long tail of long outputs, and do you reuse prompts heavily?
[07:15] Laura Bennett: Peak hours are 14:00-18:00 UTC, peak factor ~1.7x. Our generation prompts include a long policy preamble (~300 tokens) plus user query. So prefix caching could be high benefit. Reranking jobs are batched overnight and are large but tolerant latency.
[07:36] Tom Alvarez: For rerank we can tolerate higher latency and favor cheap quantized instances.
[07:40] Ethan Park: Good. For prefix caching, if the 300-token prefix repeats exactly, that's a huge win - we can reuse KV cache state. If it's templated with minor variations, hit rate drops. We'll ask for a sample of prompts to estimate effective hit rate.
[07:58] Priya Shah: What about tooling - in Console can we see token-level cost per route?
[08:03] Maya Chen: Yes Console provides per-route token cost, p95 latency, and trace hooks. You can attach token-level labels to associate cost with product features. That makes it easier to optimize.
[08:15] Laura Bennett: Are there any hidden fees for dedicated - like management, overage charges?
[08:20] Ethan Park: Overage/burst pricing is explicit in the contract. There's a management fee for Private on-prem deployments. For Dedicated we include autoscale config and burst buffer; there's an agreed rate for burst which is higher than committed unit cost. We'll put those numbers in the proposal.
[08:38] Tom Alvarez: For benchmarking, can you run a sample on our dataset? We want throughput numbers for our median and p95 workloads.
[08:45] Maya Chen: Yes - typical pilot: we run a small benchmark on Redwood hosted for quick numbers, then a Dedicated proof-of-concept to show real throughput under commit. We'll need a sample query set and test tokens.
[08:57] Laura Bennett: Ok we can share a 1K-query sample and a 7-day histogram.
[09:02] Ethan Park: Great. A note on metrics: effective cost per token = provider unit price * (1 - caching savings) * (1 - batching savings) adjusted for percent served from committed vs burst. We'll include an example calc in the spreadsheet.
[09:20] Maya Chen: Also we want to highlight that embeddings have different economics - embedding CPUs vs GPU can be cheaper in some configs; dedicated embedding nodes differ.
[09:30] Tom Alvarez: Right, we run embeddings for search index updates. They are batch and can be scheduled. Good candidate for cheaper reserved capacity.
[09:37] Priya Shah: On the security piece - will Dedicated still have Redwood-managed control plane?
[09:42] Ethan Park: For Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools and a dedicated tenant; the control plane can be Redwood-hosted or a private control plane option. For Private you manage the control plane; that's the on-prem/VPC mode.
[09:56] Laura Bennett: For contract conversations - what's a typical committed minimum? We are early stage but token volumes are meaningful; want to understand ramp.
[10:05] Maya Chen: Commit sizes vary; many customers start with a 3-6 month commit sized to their steady state. We tailor the commit so break-even is within the contract period. We'll model ramping in the spreadsheet.
[10:18] Tom Alvarez: Can you also share quantization impact on quality metrics - like rouge/accuracy deltas? We need to run an eval.
[10:26] Ethan Park: Yes, we recommend running a small eval set; our Applied ML team can help if needed. Quantization effect is model and prompt dependent.
[10:35] Laura Bennett: Anything else on cost levers we should be thinking of?
[10:38] Maya Chen: Two more: 1) route-level fallbacks - route lower-cost model for non-critical requests automatically, 2) rerating long conversations to only compute deltas via KV cache rather than full context.
[10:51] (crosstalk)
[11:05] Tom Alvarez: On SLA side - can Dedicated provide p99 SLA?
[11:08] Ethan Park: SLA levels are contractual. Dedicated + reserved pools with redundancy and failover can provide strong latencies; p99 guarantees depend on topology and geo-redundancy. We'll include typical SLA language.
[11:20] Laura Bennett: What's the timeline for a pilot?
[11:23] Maya Chen: We can get a pilot running in 2-3 weeks - hosted benchmarks same week, Dedicated POC 2-3 weeks depending on provisioning and access.
[11:33] Priya Shah: Ok good. Anything else from Redwood?
[11:36] Ethan Park: We'll prepare a cost model spreadsheet that shows hosted baseline, caching/batching assumptions, dedicated commit scenarios, and break-even graphs. We'll also include sample throughput numbers for typical 7B/13B models and quantized variants.
[11:55] Laura Bennett: Sounds good. One more question - if we commit and later need to scale down, what's the process?
[12:02] Maya Chen: Contracts can include ramp clauses; we also support credits for long-term relationships and migration assistance. We'll map the options in the proposal.
[12:12] Tom Alvarez: Great.
[12:18] [Longer jump in transcript, summarizing later points]
[30:05] Maya Chen: Revisiting the numbers - summary: send spreadsheet, get sample queries, run hosted bench then Dedicated POC.
[30:18] Laura Bennett: We'll share the data by Friday.
[30:25] Ethan Park: For the Dedicated unit-cost example I'll attach a worksheet: assumed commit covers 70% steady state, quantized models used for background rerank, peak burst handled by cloud fallback. That yields about ~2.5x improvement vs naive hosted list price in our example.
[31:00] Tom Alvarez: Good. Please include the assumptions explicitly (hit rate, batch size, quantization ratio).
[31:08] Maya Chen: Absolutely.
[31:15] Priya Shah: Anything about legal/procurement we should flag now?
[31:20] Maya Chen: Procurement items: SOC2 attestation, DPAs, encryption controls. For Private we'd go into SLAs and support tier. We'll send standard security docs.
[31:33] Laura Bennett: Ok thanks.
[31:36] Ethan Park: Quick technical note - KV cache isn't magic: for it to help you either need identical prefixes or templated prefixes with tokens that can be normalized. We can help run a prompt-variance analysis.
[31:53] Tom Alvarez: We'll include that in the sample.
[32:00] Maya Chen: Any other open questions?
[32:05] Laura Bennett: No, that covers it.
[32:09] Maya Chen: Recap of next steps: one, Maya sends cost model + security docs by 2026-03-06. Two, customer shares sample query set and 7-day histogram by 2026-03-06. Three, schedule Dedicated sizing call (Ethan + Laura) for week of 2026-03-09. Four, Redwood to run hosted benchmark once sample is received.
[32:35] Priya Shah: Agreed.
[32:38] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with a calendar invite for the sizing call.
[32:44] Laura Bennett: Thanks all.
[47:45] (meeting ends)
